en: The national flower sampaguita blooms year-round, and its white petals release a strong fragrance most noticeably during the cool evening hours.
The Ifugao people built the Banaue Rice Terraces by carving mountain steps, using an ancient irrigation system fed by surrounding rainforests.
Marine biologist Angel Alcala pioneered coral reef restoration in the Philippines, showing that protected marine sanctuaries visibly increase local fish populations.
During the Lucban Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate house exteriors with kiping, which are colorful, leaf-shaped rice wafers dried under the sun.
The Philippine eagle, our national bird, needs large dipterocarp forests to hunt monkeys and build massive nests high in the trees.
During his exile in Dapitan, Jose Rizal collected and classified local plant specimens, establishing a botanical garden to study native flora.
T'boli weavers create traditional t'nalak cloth by extracting fibers from the abaca plant, dyeing them using natural roots and leaves.
The carabao, our national animal, has a sparse hair coat and relies on wallowing in mud to cool its body in hot weather.
Botanist Leon Ma. Guerrero successfully propagated the rare waling-waling orchid, allowing this beautiful flower to be cultivated outside its native cloud forests.
The Tagbanua people of Palawan practice environmental conservation by strictly protecting their ancestral coral reefs and forests from overfishing and illegal logging.
Before paper, early Filipinos wrote the Baybayin script on natural materials like bamboo tubes, palm leaves, and tree bark using sharp styluses.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources enforces laws that visibly protect local watersheds, ensuring clean water flows into community rivers and dams.
